title: Swedish 'Great Noise': Mass Witch Panic with Children as Accusers
description: The Swedish witch persecution of 1668–1676, known as det stora oljudet ('the Great Noise'), was the largest Scandinavian witch-hunt and one of the last major European mass persecutions. Beginning in Dalarna province, the panic spread across Sweden as children accused adults of carrying them to a sabbath at 'Blåkulla' — a mythical mountain. State commissions were established and royal authority deployed; several hundred people were executed, with estimates ranging from 300 to 500 over the full period. The decisive role of child accusers — particularly children who claimed to have been taken to Blåkulla — parallels the Salem trials' use of afflicted girls twenty years later and raises similar questions about the nature and reliability of child testimony in witch proceedings.
historiographical_note: Bengt Ankarloo's work on Swedish witch trials in Witchcraft and Magic in Europe (1990, co-edited with Henningsen) is the principal English-language study. The Swedish case is notable for its late date and its distinctive Blåkulla mythology — showing that regional folk beliefs shaped the specific form witch persecution took, even within a shared European framework of diabolism.
source_method: Swedish state commission records; Ankarloo in Witchcraft and Magic in Europe (1990); secondary scholarship on Scandinavian witch-hunting
